category_title: Students who engage in disruptive off-task behavior to access peer attention
minimal_context: Craig is supposed to be completing a reading assignment during independent work time in a general classroom setting with cluster seating.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please start your independent work on the reading assignment. We will be working quietly for the next fifteen minutes.

STUDENT: (Turns to a peer at his cluster) Did you guys watch that new movie that came out yesterday?

TUTOR: Craig, remember the rules for independent work.

STUDENT: Okay. (Pauses, then leans over to another peer) Are you going to the park after school?

TUTOR: Craig, you need to stop talking and do your work.

STUDENT: (Laughs as a peer responds back) I know, right? Hey, what level did you get to on that game last night?

options.A: Provide the student with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation during independent work time, such as giving him a squishy, stress-relief ball to use at his cluster.
options.B: Implement relatively tight timelines for completing the reading assignment and other tasks during independent work time, ensuring the student understands the schedule for the session.
options.C: Proactively contact parents (using a translator if needed) to share both successes and concerns regarding the student's behavior during independent work time and other classroom activities.
options.D: Provide clear signals for talk and no-talk times using color-coded signs (green for talk, red for quiet), placing these visuals in classroom zones to indicate quiet work areas during independent work.
